title: Recurrence relations
summary: How to model counting problems with recurrences and how to solve linear recurrences with constant coefficients: the characteristic equation, distinct and repeated roots, higher degree, and nonhomogeneous recurrences including the resonance case. A final typically asks you to set up a recurrence from a counting problem and to solve one with initial conditions.

blocks.text: A recurrence defines each term of a sequence from earlier terms. Add enough starting values and the whole sequence is determined.

items: Recurrence relation: a rule giving an in terms of a0, …, an−1. Example: an = an−1 + 3.
Initial conditions: the first few terms, given outright. Example: a0 = 2.
Solution: any sequence that satisfies the rule. A closed form is a direct formula for an, like an = 2 + 3n.

blocks.text: To check a proposed closed form, plug it into the rule and the initial conditions. Or just compute the first few terms both ways and compare.
Example (iterate to guess a formula). an = an−1 + 3, a0 = 2: terms 2, 5, 8, 11, … Each step adds 3, so an = 2 + 3n.
A degree-k recurrence (an uses the previous k terms) needs k initial conditions. One is not enough for an = an−1 + an−2.

blocks.title: Verify a closed form by substitution
blocks.prompt: Show that aₙ = n·2ⁿ satisfies aₙ = 4aₙ₋₁ − 4aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 0, a₁ = 2.
steps: Initial conditions: 0 · 2⁰ = 0 and 1 · 2¹ = 2. ✓
2(n − 1) − (n − 2) = n, so the right side is n·2ⁿ = aₙ. ✓
Since the recurrence plus two initial values determines the sequence, this is the solution.
blocks.answer: aₙ = n·2ⁿ satisfies both the recurrence and the initial conditions

lesson.title: Setting up recurrences from counting problems

blocks.text: Ask: “How does a size-n object break into smaller ones?” Usually you split by the last step (or first step) and count each case using smaller sizes.
Example (compound interest). An account starts at 1000 and earns 5% a year. If Pₙ is the amount after n years, Pₙ = 1.05Pₙ₋₁, P₀ = 1000, so Pₙ = 1000 · 1.05ⁿ (about 1628.89 after 10 years).

blocks.title: Tower of Hanoi
blocks.prompt: Move n disks from peg 1 to peg 3, never putting a larger disk on a smaller one. H<sub>n</sub> = minimum moves.
steps: Move the top n − 1 disks out of the way: H<sub>n−1</sub> moves.
Move the biggest disk: 1 move.
Move the n − 1 disks back on top of it: H<sub>n−1</sub> moves.
H<sub>n</sub> = 2H<sub>n−1</sub> + 1, H<sub>1</sub> = 1. Terms: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 … which looks like 2<sup>n</sup> − 1.

blocks.title: Bit strings with no two consecutive 0s
blocks.prompt: an = number of length-n bit strings with no “00”. Split by the last bit:
steps: Ends in 1: the first n − 1 bits can be any valid string. That’s an−1 strings.
Ends in 0: the bit before it must be 1 (otherwise “00”), so the string ends “10” and the first n − 2 bits are any valid string. That’s an−2 strings.
The cases don’t overlap, so add them (sum rule): a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub> + a<sub>n−2</sub>.
Initial conditions by hand: a<sub>1</sub> = 2 (0, 1) and a<sub>2</sub> = 3 (01, 10, 11).
Then a<sub>3</sub> = 5, a<sub>4</sub> = 8, a<sub>5</sub> = 13: Fibonacci numbers.
blocks.answer: aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂, a₁ = 2, a₂ = 3 (Fibonacci numbers)

blocks.title: Climbing stairs
blocks.prompt: You climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Let sₙ be the number of ways. Find a recurrence and s₁₀.
steps: Split by the last move: a 1-step leaves n − 1 stairs (sₙ₋₁ ways); a 2-step leaves n − 2 stairs (sₙ₋₂ ways).
sₙ = sₙ₋₁ + sₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 3, with s₁ = 1, s₂ = 2 (1+1 or 2).
With steps of 1, 2 or 3 the same idea gives sₙ = sₙ₋₁ + sₙ₋₂ + sₙ₋₃ (1, 2, 4, 7, 13, …).
blocks.answer: sₙ = sₙ₋₁ + sₙ₋₂, s₁ = 1, s₂ = 2; s₁₀ = 89

blocks.title: Domino tilings of a 2 × n board
blocks.prompt: Let tₙ be the number of ways to tile a 2 × n board with 1 × 2 dominoes. Find a recurrence.
steps: Look at the right end. Either one vertical domino covers the last column: tₙ₋₁ ways for the rest.
Or a horizontal domino covers the top of the last two columns; then another horizontal domino must sit directly below it: tₙ₋₂ ways for the rest.
These cases are disjoint and cover everything: tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + tₙ₋₂, with t₁ = 1, t₂ = 2.

blocks.title: Regions cut by lines
blocks.prompt: n lines are drawn in the plane, no two parallel and no three through one point. Let Rₙ be the number of regions. Find a recurrence and solve it.
steps: R₀ = 1 (the whole plane).
The n-th line crosses the other n − 1 lines in n − 1 distinct points, which cut it into n pieces.
Each piece splits one old region into two, so Rₙ = Rₙ₋₁ + n.
blocks.answer: Rₙ = Rₙ₋₁ + n, R₀ = 1; Rₙ = (n² + n + 2)/2

blocks.text: Check that your cases are disjoint and cover everything, and compute the initial conditions by actually listing small cases.

lesson.title: Linear homogeneous recurrences and the characteristic equation

blocks.text: For a certain nice kind of recurrence, guessing a<sub>n</sub> = r<sup>n</sup> turns the whole problem into solving a polynomial.
a<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>a<sub>n−1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub>a<sub>n−2</sub> + ⋯ + c<sub>k</sub>a<sub>n−k</sub>

Linear: each earlier term appears to the first power, multiplied by a number. Homogeneous: no extra term that isn’t a multiple of some aj. Constant coefficients: the c’s are fixed numbers, not depending on n. Degree k (with ck ≠ 0).
Where the characteristic equation comes from

blocks.title: Method
items: Guess a<sub>n</sub> = r<sup>n</sup> in a<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>a<sub>n−1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub>a<sub>n−2</sub>.
You get r<sup>n</sup> = c<sub>1</sub>r<sup>n−1</sup> + c<sub>2</sub>r<sup>n−2</sup>.
Divide by r<sup>n−2</sup>: r² = c<sub>1</sub>r + c<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.text: r² − c<sub>1</sub>r − c<sub>2</sub> = 0
The characteristic equation. Its solutions are the characteristic roots. Each root r gives a solution rn.
Fast way to write it: replace a<sub>n</sub> by r<sup>k</sup>, a<sub>n−1</sub> by r<sup>k−1</sup>, …, a<sub>n−k</sub> by 1, then move everything to one side.
For a<sub>n</sub> = 5a<sub>n−1</sub> − 6a<sub>n−2</sub> the equation is r² − 5r + 6 = 0. Both signs flip when you move the terms over.
roots r<sub>1</sub> ≠ r<sub>2</sub> ⟹ a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>r<sub>1</sub><sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>r<sub>2</sub><sup>n</sup>

blocks.name: Distinct roots give every solution
blocks.text: If r² − c₁r − c₂ = 0 has distinct roots r₁ ≠ r₂, then {aₙ} solves aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ if and only if aₙ = α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ for some constants α₁, α₂.

proof.text: These are solutions. c₁rᵢⁿ⁻¹ + c₂rᵢⁿ⁻² = rᵢⁿ⁻²(c₁rᵢ + c₂) = rᵢⁿ⁻²·rᵢ² = rᵢⁿ, because rᵢ is a root. A linear combination of solutions is again a solution, since the recurrence is linear.

They are all the solutions. Given any solution, choose α₁, α₂ with α₁ + α₂ = a₀ and α₁r₁ + α₂r₂ = a₁. This system has the unique solution α₁ = (a₁ − a₀r₂)/(r₁ − r₂), α₂ = (a₀r₁ − a₁)/(r₁ − r₂); dividing by r₁ − r₂ is where r₁ ≠ r₂ is used.
Then α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ and aₙ satisfy the same recurrence and agree at n = 0, 1, so by strong induction they agree for all n.

blocks.text: Every solution has this form. The constants α<sub>1</sub>, α<sub>2</sub> are pinned down by the two initial conditions.
The recipe

blocks.title: Method
items: Write the characteristic equation and find its roots.
Write the general form a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>r<sub>1</sub><sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>r<sub>2</sub><sup>n</sup>.
Plug in n = 0 and n = 1 (or whichever initial conditions you’re given) to get two equations.
Solve for α<sub>1</sub>, α<sub>2</sub>.
Check by computing a2 from the recurrence and from your formula.

blocks.title: Two distinct roots
steps: a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>2<sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>3<sup>n</sup>.
n = 0: α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub> = 1. n = 1: 2α<sub>1</sub> + 3α<sub>2</sub> = 4.
Subtract twice the first from the second: α<sub>2</sub> = 2, then α<sub>1</sub> = −1.
an = 2·3n − 2n. Check: recurrence gives a2 = 20 − 6 = 14; formula gives 18 − 4 = 14. ✓

blocks.title: A negative root
blocks.prompt: Solve aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 7.
steps: α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub> = 2 and 2α<sub>1</sub> − α<sub>2</sub> = 7. Adding: 3α<sub>1</sub> = 9, so α<sub>1</sub> = 3, α<sub>2</sub> = −1.
an = 3·2n − (−1)n. Check a2: 7 + 4 = 11 and 12 − 1 = 11. ✓

blocks.title: Fibonacci: irrational roots
blocks.prompt: Solve fₙ = fₙ₋₁ + fₙ₋₂ with f₀ = 0, f₁ = 1.
steps: Characteristic equation r² − r − 1 = 0, roots r₁ = (1 + √5)/2, r₂ = (1 − √5)/2.
n = 0: α₁ + α₂ = 0. n = 1: α₁r₁ + α₂r₂ = 1.
So α₂ = −α₁ and α₁(r₁ − r₂) = 1; since r₁ − r₂ = √5, α₁ = 1/√5.
Irrational roots are fine; the recipe is identical.

blocks.text: A degree-k recurrence needs k different solutions to fit k initial conditions. If the characteristic equation has fewer than k different roots, a repeated root supplies the missing ones by multiplying by powers of n.

If both roots are the same number r<sub>0</sub>, then α<sub>1</sub>r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup> is really just one term, which can’t fit two initial conditions. The fix: the second solution is n·r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup>.
double root r<sub>0</sub> ⟹ a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>·n·r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup> = (α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub>n) r<sub>0</sub><sup>n</sup>

blocks.name: Why n·r₀ⁿ is a solution
blocks.text: If r₀ is a double root of r² − c₁r − c₂, then n·r₀ⁿ solves aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂, so every solution is (α₁ + α₂n)r₀ⁿ.

proof.text: A double root means r² − c₁r − c₂ = (r − r₀)², so c₁ = 2r₀ and c₂ = −r₀².
c₁(n − 1)r₀ⁿ⁻¹ + c₂(n − 2)r₀ⁿ⁻² = r₀ⁿ⁻²[2r₀²(n − 1) − r₀²(n − 2)] = r₀ⁿ⁻² · r₀² · n = n·r₀ⁿ
So n·r₀ⁿ is a solution, and r₀ⁿ is one too. The system α₁ = a₀, (α₁ + α₂)r₀ = a₁ always has a unique solution when r₀ ≠ 0, so as in the distinct case these give every solution.

blocks.text: You spot a repeated root when the quadratic is a perfect square, like r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)².

blocks.title: Double root
steps: r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)² = 0: double root r<sub>0</sub> = 2.
a<sub>n</sub> = (α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub>n)2<sup>n</sup>.
an = (1 + 2n)2n. Check a2: 24 − 4 = 20 and 5·4 = 20. ✓

blocks.title: Double root, second example
steps: r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)² = 0: root 2, repeated twice.
General solution: a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>2<sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>n2<sup>n</sup>.
a<sub>0</sub> = 2 gives α<sub>1</sub> = 2. a<sub>1</sub> = 12 gives 12 = 2·2 + α<sub>2</sub>·2, so α<sub>2</sub> = 4.
an = 2·2n + 4n·2n. Check a2: 48 − 8 = 40 and 8 + 32 = 40. ✓

blocks.title: Double root at 1
blocks.prompt: Solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ − aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 4.
steps: r² − 2r + 1 = (r − 1)² = 0: root 1, repeated twice.
a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>·1<sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>n·1<sup>n</sup> = α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub>n.
α<sub>1</sub> = 2, and 4 = 2 + α<sub>2</sub>, so α<sub>2</sub> = 2.

blocks.text: Writing α1r0n + α2r0n for a repeated root. The equations will be inconsistent. You need the extra n.
Same recipe, bigger polynomial. A degree-k recurrence has a degree-k characteristic equation and needs k initial conditions.
root r with multiplicity m contributes
(α<sub>0</sub> + α<sub>1</sub>n + ⋯ + α<sub>m−1</sub>n<sup>m−1</sup>) r<sup>n</sup>
Distinct roots: m = 1, a plain αr<sup>n</sup>. Double root: (α<sub>0</sub> + α<sub>1</sub>n)r<sup>n</sup>. Triple root: up to n². Add up the contributions of all roots.

blocks.title: Degree 3, distinct roots
blocks.prompt: Solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ − 2aₙ₋₃ with a₀ = 3, a₁ = 2, a₂ = 6.
steps: r³ − 2r² − r + 2 = r²(r − 2) − (r − 2) = (r − 2)(r − 1)(r + 1). Tip: try grouping, or test small integers like r = 1 first.
a<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub>(−1)<sup>n</sup> + α<sub>3</sub>2<sup>n</sup>.

n = 0, 1, 2: α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub> + α<sub>3</sub> = 3; α<sub>1</sub> − α<sub>2</sub> + 2α<sub>3</sub> = 2; α<sub>1</sub> + α<sub>2</sub> + 4α<sub>3</sub> = 6. Subtracting the first from the third: 3α<sub>3</sub> = 3, so α<sub>3</sub> = 1; then α<sub>1</sub> = α<sub>2</sub> = 1.
an = 1 + (−1)n + 2n. Check a3: 12 + 2 − 6 = 8 and 1 − 1 + 8 = 8. ✓

blocks.title: Degree 3 with a repeated root
blocks.prompt: Solve aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ − 4aₙ₋₃ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 3, a₂ = 13.
steps: Characteristic equation r³ − 3r² + 4 = 0. Test small integers: r = −1 gives −1 − 3 + 4 = 0.
Divide by r + 1: r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)². Roots −1 and 2 (double).
General form aₙ = γ(−1)ⁿ + (α + βn)2ⁿ.
Subtract the first from the third: 3α + 8β = 11. Add the first two: 3α + 2β = 5. So 6β = 6, β = 1, α = 1, γ = 1.

blocks.text: When there’s an extra term F(n) (like the +1 in Hanoi), find one solution that handles F(n), then add the general solution of the recurrence without F(n).
a<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>a<sub>n−1</sub> + ⋯ + c<sub>k</sub>a<sub>n−k</sub> + F(n)
all solutions = a<sub>n</sub><sup>(p)</sup> + a<sub>n</sub><sup>(h)</sup>
(p) = one particular solution. (h) = general solution of the associated homogeneous recurrence (drop F(n)).
The recipe

blocks.title: Method
items: Solve the homogeneous part (drop F(n)) to get a<sub>n</sub><sup>(h)</sup> with unknown α’s.
Guess a particular solution shaped like F(n), with unknown coefficients (table below). Plug it in and solve for them.
Add the two, then use the initial conditions to find the α’s.

head: F(n)
Try
rows: polynomial of degree d, like An + B
s<sup>n</sup>, s a root of multiplicity m

blocks.title: Constant forcing: Tower of Hanoi
steps: Homogeneous: H<sub>n</sub> = 2H<sub>n−1</sub> → α·2<sup>n</sup>.
F(n) = 1 is constant, so try A: A = 2A + 1 → A = −1.
General: H<sub>n</sub> = α·2<sup>n</sup> − 1. H<sub>1</sub> = 1 gives 2α − 1 = 1, α = 1.
Hn = 2n − 1, matching 1, 3, 7, 15, … ✓

blocks.title: Polynomial forcing
steps: Homogeneous: α·3<sup>n</sup>.
F(n) = 2n is degree 1, so try cn + d: cn + d = 3(c(n−1) + d) + 2n. Match the n terms: c = 3c + 2 → c = −1. Match constants: d = −3c + 3d → d = −3/2.
General: a<sub>n</sub> = α·3<sup>n</sup> − n − 3/2. a<sub>1</sub> = 3 gives 3α − 5/2 = 3, α = 11/6.

blocks.title: Exponential forcing, no resonance
steps: Homogeneous: α·3ⁿ.
F(n) = 2ⁿ and 2 is not a root, so try A·2ⁿ: A·2ⁿ = 3A·2ⁿ⁻¹ + 2ⁿ. Divide by 2ⁿ⁻¹: 2A = 3A + 2, so A = −2.
General: aₙ = α·3ⁿ − 2·2ⁿ. a₀ = 1 gives α − 2 = 1, α = 3.
Check a₁ = 3 · 1 + 2 = 5 and 9 − 4 = 5. ✓

blocks.title: Resonance: the forcing base is a root
steps: Homogeneous: roots 2 and 3, so α·2ⁿ + β·3ⁿ.
F(n) = 2ⁿ and 2 is a root of multiplicity 1, so A·2ⁿ cannot work (it solves the homogeneous part). Try A·n·2ⁿ.
Plug in and divide by 2ⁿ⁻²: 4An = 10A(n − 1) − 6A(n − 2) + 4 = 4An + 2A + 4, so A = −2.
General: aₙ = α·2ⁿ + β·3ⁿ − 2n·2ⁿ. n = 0: α + β = 1. n = 1: 2α + 3β − 4 = 0.

blocks.title: Constant forcing on a degree-2 recurrence
blocks.prompt: Solve aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2aₙ₋₂ + 4 with a₀ = 0, a₁ = 1.
steps: Homogeneous: r² − r − 2 = (r − 2)(r + 1), so α·2ⁿ + β(−1)ⁿ.
1 is not a root, so try a constant A: A = A + 2A + 4, A = −2.

blocks.text: Use the initial conditions after adding the particular solution, never on the homogeneous part alone.

cards.front: What is a recurrence relation? What are initial conditions, a solution and a closed form?

items: Recurrence relation: a rule giving aₙ in terms of earlier terms a₀, …, aₙ₋₁. Example: aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3.
Initial conditions: the first few terms, given outright. Example: a₀ = 2.
Solution: any sequence that obeys the rule.
Closed form: a direct formula for aₙ, with no earlier terms.

back.text: Example. aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3, a₀ = 2 gives 2, 5, 8, 11, … Each step adds 3, so the closed form is aₙ = 2 + 3n.

cards.front: How many initial conditions does a recurrence need? How do you check a proposed closed form?

back.text: If aₙ depends on the previous k terms (degree k), you need k initial conditions. aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ needs two, like a₀ and a₁.

items: It must match the initial conditions.
It must satisfy the rule. A quick check: compute the next term from the recurrence and from the formula, and compare.

cards.front: How do you set up a recurrence for a counting problem?

items: Let aₙ = the answer for size n.
Split the size-n objects into cases by their last step (or first step): last bit, last move, last year, …
Count each case using smaller sizes (aₙ₋₁, aₙ₋₂, …).
Make sure the cases are disjoint and cover everything, then add them (sum rule).
Find the initial conditions by listing small cases by hand.

cards.front: $1000 earns 5% interest per year. Write a recurrence and a closed form.

back.text: Pₙ = amount after n years. Each year you keep Pₙ₋₁ and gain 5% of it:

cards.front: Tower of Hanoi: find a recurrence for Hₙ, the minimum moves to move n disks.

back.text: Rules: move one disk at a time, never put a bigger disk on a smaller one.

items: Move the top n − 1 disks to the spare peg: Hₙ₋₁ moves.
Move the biggest disk to the target: 1 move.
Move the n − 1 disks onto it: Hₙ₋₁ moves.

back.text: Terms: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, … which looks like 2ⁿ − 1 (proved on a later card).

cards.front: Find a recurrence for aₙ = number of bit strings of length n with no two consecutive 0s.

items: Ends in 1: the first n − 1 bits are any valid string: aₙ₋₁ ways.
Ends in 0: the bit before must be 1 (else “00”), so it ends “10” and the first n − 2 bits are any valid string: aₙ₋₂ ways.

back.text: a₁: 0, 1. a₂: 01, 10, 11. Then a₃ = 5, a₄ = 8, a₅ = 13: Fibonacci numbers.

cards.front: What is a linear homogeneous recurrence relation of degree k with constant coefficients?

items: Linear: each earlier term appears to the first power, times a number. No squares, no products of terms.
Homogeneous: no extra term that isn’t a multiple of some aⱼ (no “+1”, no “+2n”).
Constant coefficients: the c’s are fixed numbers, not depending on n.
Degree k: reaches back k terms.

back.text: These are exactly the recurrences the characteristic equation can solve.

cards.front: Which are linear homogeneous with constant coefficients? (a) aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ (b) aₙ = aₙ₋₅ (c) aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂² (d) Hₙ = 2Hₙ₋₁ + 1 (e) Bₙ = nBₙ₋₁

items: Yes, degree 2.
Yes, degree 5.
No: not linear (squared term).
No: not homogeneous (the +1).
No: the coefficient n isn’t constant.

cards.front: What is the characteristic equation, and where does it come from?

items: Guess aₙ = rⁿ in aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂.
You get rⁿ = c₁rⁿ⁻¹ + c₂rⁿ⁻².
Divide by rⁿ⁻²: r² = c₁r + c₂.

back.text: Its solutions are the characteristic roots. Each root r gives a solution rⁿ.
Fast way. Replace aₙ by rᵏ, aₙ₋₁ by rᵏ⁻¹, …, aₙ₋ₖ by 1, then move everything to one side.

cards.front: Write the characteristic equation of aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂.

back.text: Both signs flip when you move the terms to the left. Writing r² + 5r − 6 is the classic mistake.

cards.front: How do you solve aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ when the characteristic equation has two different roots r₁, r₂?

back.text: Every solution has this form; the initial conditions pin down α₁ and α₂.

items: Write the characteristic equation and find its roots.
Write the general form aₙ = α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ.
Plug in the two initial conditions (usually n = 0 and n = 1) to get two equations.
Solve for α₁, α₂.
Check: compute a₂ from the recurrence and from your formula.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 5aₙ₋₁ − 6aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 4.

items: aₙ = α₁2ⁿ + α₂3ⁿ.
Subtract twice the first from the second: α₂ = 2, so α₁ = −1.

cards.front: solve aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 7.

items: aₙ = α₁2ⁿ + α₂(−1)ⁿ.
α₁ + α₂ = 2 and 2α₁ − α₂ = 7. Add them: 3α₁ = 9, so α₁ = 3, α₂ = −1.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 7aₙ₋₁ − 10aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 7.

items: α₁ + α₂ = 2 and 2α₁ + 5α₂ = 7, so α₂ = 1 and α₁ = 1.

cards.front: Fibonacci: fₙ = fₙ₋₁ + fₙ₋₂, f₀ = 0, f₁ = 1. What are the characteristic roots and the closed form?

back.text: r² − r − 1 = 0, so r = (1 ± √5)/2 by the quadratic formula. Solving for the α’s from f₀ = 0, f₁ = 1 gives α₁ = 1/√5, α₂ = −1/√5:
Irrational roots are fine; the recipe is identical.

cards.front: How do you solve a degree-2 recurrence when the characteristic equation has only one (repeated) root r₀?

back.text: Why the extra n. α₁r₀ⁿ + α₂r₀ⁿ is really just one term (α₁ + α₂)r₀ⁿ, which can’t fit two initial conditions. The second independent solution turns out to be n·r₀ⁿ.
How to spot it. The quadratic is a perfect square, like r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)².
Forgetting the n: the equations for α₁, α₂ come out inconsistent.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 4aₙ₋₁ − 4aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 6.

items: r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)² = 0: double root 2.
aₙ = (α₁ + α₂n)2ⁿ.

cards.front: solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ − aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 2, a₁ = 4.

items: r² − 2r + 1 = (r − 1)²: double root 1.
aₙ = (α₁ + α₂n)·1ⁿ = α₁ + α₂n. α₁ = 2; 2 + α₂ = 4, so α₂ = 2.

back.text: Check: 2, 4, 6, 8, … and 2·4 − 2 = 6 ✓. A root of 1 makes 1ⁿ = 1, so the answer is just a line.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = −6aₙ₋₁ − 9aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 0.

items: r² + 6r + 9 = (r + 3)²: double root −3.

cards.front: What is the general solution for higher degree, including repeated roots?

back.text: Same recipe, bigger polynomial. Degree k → degree-k characteristic equation → k initial conditions.
root r of multiplicity m contributes (α₀ + α₁n + ⋯ + αₘ₋₁nᵐ⁻¹)·rⁿ
Add up the contributions of all the roots. A simple root (m = 1) gives αrⁿ; a double root gives (α₀ + α₁n)rⁿ; a triple root goes up to n².
The total number of α’s always equals the degree k.

cards.front: The characteristic roots are 2, 2, 2 and 5. What is the general form of aₙ?

back.text: 2 has multiplicity 3 (up to n²), and 5 is simple. That’s four constants for a degree-4 recurrence.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ − 2aₙ₋₃ with a₀ = 3, a₁ = 2, a₂ = 6.

items: aₙ = α₁ + α₂(−1)ⁿ + α₃2ⁿ.
n = 0, 1, 2: α₁ + α₂ + α₃ = 3; α₁ − α₂ + 2α₃ = 2; α₁ + α₂ + 4α₃ = 6. Subtract the first from the third: 3α₃ = 3, so α₃ = 1, then α₁ = α₂ = 1.

cards.front: What is a linear nonhomogeneous recurrence, and what do all its solutions look like?

back.text: F(n) is an extra term that isn’t a multiple of any aⱼ, like the +1 in Hanoi. Dropping it gives the associated homogeneous recurrence.
aₙ⁽ᵖ⁾ is one particular solution of the full recurrence. aₙ⁽ʰ⁾ is the general solution of the homogeneous one, with its α’s still unknown.

cards.front: What is the recipe for a nonhomogeneous recurrence, and what do you guess for the particular solution?

items: Solve the homogeneous part (drop F(n)) to get aₙ⁽ʰ⁾ with unknown α’s.
Guess a particular solution shaped like F(n) with unknown coefficients; plug in and solve for them.
Add the two, then use the initial conditions to find the α’s.
F(n) constant → try A.
F(n) polynomial of degree d (like 2n) → polynomial of degree d (An + B).
F(n) = sⁿ, s not a characteristic root → A·sⁿ.
F(n) = sⁿ, s a root of multiplicity m → A·nᵐ·sⁿ.

back.text: Using the initial conditions on the homogeneous part alone, before adding the particular solution.

cards.front: Solve the Tower of Hanoi recurrence Hₙ = 2Hₙ₋₁ + 1 with H₁ = 1.

items: Homogeneous Hₙ = 2Hₙ₋₁: root 2, so α·2ⁿ.
F(n) = 1 is constant; try A: A = 2A + 1, so A = −1.
General: Hₙ = α·2ⁿ − 1. H₁ = 1 gives 2α − 1 = 1, so α = 1.

cards.front: solve aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2n with a₁ = 3.

items: Homogeneous: α·3ⁿ.
F(n) = 2n has degree 1, so try cn + d: cn + d = 3(c(n − 1) + d) + 2n.
Match n terms: c = 3c + 2, so c = −1. Match constants: d = −3c + 3d, so 2d = 3c and d = −3/2.
General: aₙ = α·3ⁿ − n − 3/2. a₁ = 3 gives 3α − 5/2 = 3, so α = 11/6.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 3 with a₀ = 1.

items: Homogeneous: α·2ⁿ.
Particular: A = 2A + 3, so A = −3.
General: α·2ⁿ − 3. a₀ = 1 gives α − 3 = 1, so α = 4.

cards.front: Why do repeated characteristic roots need a special fix, and what is it?

back.text: The problem. A degree-k recurrence needs k different solutions so the α’s can match k initial conditions. If a root r is repeated, rⁿ only counts once, leaving you short.
root r repeated m times ⟹ rⁿ, n·rⁿ, …, nᵐ⁻¹rⁿ are all solutions
For a double root r₀ of a degree-2 recurrence: aₙ = α₁r₀ⁿ + α₂·n·r₀ⁿ.
Writing α₁r₀ⁿ + α₂r₀ⁿ. That’s really one term, (α₁ + α₂)r₀ⁿ, and can’t fit two initial conditions.

cards.front: Solve aₙ = 8aₙ₋₁ − 16aₙ₋₂ with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 8.

items: r² − 8r + 16 = (r − 4)²: root 4 twice.
aₙ = (α₁ + α₂n)4ⁿ. α₁ = 1; (1 + α₂)·4 = 8, so α₂ = 1.

cards.front: Why is every solution of a linear homogeneous recurrence (distinct roots) a combination α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ?

back.text: Each rᵢⁿ solves it (plug in and use rᵢ² = c₁rᵢ + c₂), combinations of solutions are solutions, and any two initial values can be matched because r₁ ≠ r₂. A sequence is determined by its recurrence and initial values, so it equals the matching combination.

cards.front: Resonance: what particular solution do you try for F(n) = C·sⁿ when s is a root of multiplicity m?

back.text: If you try A·sⁿ when s is a root, you get a contradiction like A = A + 2: that is the signal to multiply by n.

cards.front: More generally, F(n) = (polynomial of degree t)·sⁿ: what is the trial particular solution?

back.text: m = multiplicity of s as a characteristic root (m = 0 if s is not a root). A plain polynomial F(n) is the case s = 1.

prompt.text: Let a<sub>n</sub> be the number of strings of length n over {0, 1, 2} with no two consecutive 0s. Find a recurrence and initial conditions, compute a<sub>4</sub>, and solve the recurrence.

solution.text: Look at the last character. If it is 1 or 2, the first n − 1 characters are any valid string: 2a<sub>n−1</sub>. If it is 0, the character before it must be 1 or 2, and the first n − 2 characters are any valid string: 2a<sub>n−2</sub>.
a<sub>n</sub> = 2a<sub>n−1</sub> + 2a<sub>n−2</sub>, a<sub>0</sub> = 1, a<sub>1</sub> = 3

The characteristic equation r² − 2r − 2 = 0 has roots r = 1 ± √3. Write a<sub>n</sub> = α(1+√3)<sup>n</sup> + β(1−√3)<sup>n</sup>. From a<sub>0</sub>: α + β = 1. From a<sub>1</sub>: (α + β) + √3(α − β) = 3, so α − β = 2/√3.
Tests: sorting by the last character, and irrational roots. Common mistake: writing 2an−1 + an−2, which forgets that the character before the final 0 has 2 choices.

prompt.text: Let t<sub>n</sub> be the number of ways to tile a 2 × n board with 1 × 2 dominoes (in either orientation) and 2 × 2 squares. Find a recurrence, solve it, and give t<sub>10</sub>.

solution.text: Look at the right end. Either a vertical domino covers the last column (t<sub>n−1</sub> ways), or the last two columns are covered by two stacked horizontal dominoes or by one 2 × 2 square (2t<sub>n−2</sub> ways). A single horizontal domino at the end forces a second one directly above or below it.
t<sub>n</sub> = t<sub>n−1</sub> + 2t<sub>n−2</sub>, t<sub>0</sub> = t<sub>1</sub> = 1
r² − r − 2 = (r − 2)(r + 1), so t<sub>n</sub> = α2<sup>n</sup> + β(−1)<sup>n</sup>. The conditions α + β = 1 and 2α − β = 1 give α = 2/3, β = 1/3.
Answer: tn = (2n+1 + (−1)n)/3, and t10 = 683.
Tests: case analysis on the right end that is exhaustive and doesn’t double count. Common mistake: counting “one horizontal domino” as a separate case of width 1.

prompt.text: Solve a<sub>n</sub> = 5a<sub>n−1</sub> − 8a<sub>n−2</sub> + 4a<sub>n−3</sub> with a<sub>0</sub> = 1, a<sub>1</sub> = 3, a<sub>2</sub> = 9.

solution.text: r³ − 5r² + 8r − 4: r = 1 is a root (1 − 5 + 8 − 4 = 0). Dividing leaves r² − 4r + 4 = (r − 2)². So the characteristic polynomial is (r − 1)(r − 2)², and a<sub>n</sub> = α + (β + γn)2<sup>n</sup>.
Subtracting consecutive equations: β + 2γ = 2 and 2β + 6γ = 6, so γ = 1, β = 0, α = 1.
Answer: an = 1 + n·2n
Tests: factoring a cubic by testing small integer roots, and handling a repeated root. Common mistake: writing α + β2n + γ2n, which has no n·2n term and is really only two parameters.

items: (a) Solve a<sub>n</sub> = 3a<sub>n−1</sub> + 2·3<sup>n</sup>, a<sub>0</sub> = 1.
(b) Solve a<sub>n</sub> = 2a<sub>n−1</sub> + n, a<sub>0</sub> = 0.

solution.text: (a) The homogeneous part gives α3n. The forcing term 2·3n uses 3, which is a root of multiplicity 1, so try pn = Cn3n: Cn3n = 3C(n−1)3n−1 + 2·3n. Dividing by 3n: Cn = C(n − 1) + 2, so C = 2. With a0 = 1, α = 1. an = (1 + 2n)3n.

(b) Try pn = cn + d: cn + d = 2c(n − 1) + 2d + n. Comparing n-coefficients: c = 2c + 1, so c = −1. Comparing constants: d = −2c + 2d, so d = 2c = −2. Then an = α2n − n − 2, and a0 = 0 gives α = 2. an = 2n+1 − n − 2.
Tests: when the forcing base is a characteristic root, multiply the guess by nm. Common mistake: in (a), trying C·3n, which leads to C = C + 2 (no solution). That failure is the sign of resonance.
The characteristic polynomial is (r − 2)², so 2 is a double root and the forcing base 2 resonates twice. Try p<sub>n</sub> = Cn²2<sup>n</sup>. Dividing by 2<sup>n</sup>:
Cn² = 2C(n−1)² − C(n−2)² + 1 = Cn² − 2C + 1
So C = 1/2. The general solution is a<sub>n</sub> = (α + βn + n²/2)2<sup>n</sup>. a<sub>0</sub> = 0 gives α = 0, and a<sub>1</sub> = (β + ½)·2 = 0 gives β = −½.
Answer: an = ((n² − n)/2)·2n = n(n − 1)2n−1
Tests: multiplicity 2 means the guess gets a factor n². Common mistake: using Cn2n. Its terms cancel completely, leaving 0 = 1.

prompt.text: Tower of Hanoi with three pegs in a row, A–B–C, where disks may move only between neighboring pegs (A↔B or B↔C). Find the minimum number of moves an to transfer n disks from A to C. Set up the recurrence by arguing what must happen, then solve it.

solution.text: The largest disk must go A → B → C. When it moves A → B, all n − 1 smaller disks must be on C (they can’t be on A or B). When it moves B → C, they must all be on A. So the moves are forced into this pattern:

solution.title: Method
items: n − 1 disks A → C (a<sub>n−1</sub>)
largest A → B (1)
n − 1 disks C → A (a<sub>n−1</sub>, by symmetry)
largest B → C (1)
n − 1 disks A → C (a<sub>n−1</sub>)

solution.text: a<sub>n</sub> = 3a<sub>n−1</sub> + 2, a<sub>1</sub> = 2
A constant particular solution c = 3c + 2 gives c = −1, so an = α3n − 1, and a1 = 2 gives α = 1. an = 3n − 1. (Checked by computer search for n ≤ 6.)

Tests: justifying that the structure is forced, which proves minimality, not just a count of moves. Common mistake: writing 2an−1 + 1 as in ordinary Hanoi, forgetting that the big disk now needs two moves.

hard.title: Calls made by naive recursive Fibonacci

prompt.text: Naive recursive fib(n) calls fib(n − 1) and fib(n − 2) for n ≥ 2 and returns directly for n = 0, 1. Let an be the total number of calls made by fib(n), counting the first one.

items: (a) Show that a<sub>n</sub> = a<sub>n−1</sub> + a<sub>n−2</sub> + 1 with a<sub>0</sub> = a<sub>1</sub> = 1, and prove a<sub>n</sub> = 2F<sub>n+1</sub> − 1 (F<sub>0</sub> = 0, F<sub>1</sub> = 1).
(b) Prove Cassini’s identity F<sub>n+1</sub>F<sub>n−1</sub> − F<sub>n</sub>² = (−1)<sup>n</sup> for n ≥ 1.

hard.answer: (a) aₙ = 2Fₙ₊₁ − 1 by strong induction (b) Cassini’s identity by induction using Fₙ₊₂ = Fₙ₊₁ + Fₙ

solution.text: (a) The call fib(n) itself, plus every call made by fib(n − 1), plus every call made by fib(n − 2). Bases: 2F1 − 1 = 1 and 2F2 − 1 = 1. Step (strong induction): an = (2Fn − 1) + (2Fn−1 − 1) + 1 = 2Fn+1 − 1.
(b) Base n = 1: F2F0 − F1² = 0 − 1 = −1. Step: Fn+2Fn − Fn+1² = (Fn+1 + Fn)Fn − Fn+1(Fn + Fn−1) = Fn² − Fn+1Fn−1 = −(−1)n = (−1)n+1.
Tests: guessing a closed form and confirming it by induction. Common mistake: forgetting the “+1” for the call itself.

hard.title: Why distinct roots give all solutions

prompt.text: Let r² − c1r − c2 have two distinct roots r1 ≠ r2. Prove that a sequence satisfies an = c1an−1 + c2an−2 for all n ≥ 2 if and only if an = α1r1n + α2r2n for some constants α1, α2. Point out exactly where r1 ≠ r2 is used.

hard.answer: rᵢⁿ solve it and combinations do too; α₁, α₂ matching a₀, a₁ exist because r₁ ≠ r₂ (division by r₁ − r₂); strong induction gives equality.

solution.text: (⇐) c1rin−1 + c2rin−2 = rin−2(c1ri + c2) = rin−2·ri² = rin. So each rin satisfies the recurrence, and since the recurrence is linear, so does any combination of them.
(⇒) Pick α1, α2 to match the first two terms: α1 + α2 = a0 and α1r1 + α2r2 = a1. The solution is
α<sub>1</sub> = (a<sub>1</sub> − a<sub>0</sub>r<sub>2</sub>)/(r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub>), α<sub>2</sub> = (a<sub>0</sub>r<sub>1</sub> − a<sub>1</sub>)/(r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub>)
Dividing by r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub> is exactly where r<sub>1</sub> ≠ r<sub>2</sub> is needed.

Let b<sub>n</sub> = α<sub>1</sub>r<sub>1</sub><sup>n</sup> + α<sub>2</sub>r<sub>2</sub><sup>n</sup>. By (⇐), b satisfies the same recurrence, and b<sub>0</sub> = a<sub>0</sub>, b<sub>1</sub> = a<sub>1</sub>. Strong induction: if a<sub>k</sub> = b<sub>k</sub> for all k < n (n ≥ 2), then a<sub>n</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>a<sub>n−1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub>a<sub>n−2</sub> = c<sub>1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub>b<sub>n−2</sub> = b<sub>n</sub>. ∎

Tests: the two halves (it satisfies the recurrence; it is determined by two initial values) and the role of distinct roots. Common mistake: proving only (⇐) and calling it done. That shows these are solutions, not that they are all of them.

hard.title: Solve a recurrence and model “no 01”

prompt.text: (a) Solve an = an−1 + 6an−2 with a0 = 3, a1 = 4.
(b) Let sn be the number of strings of length n over {0, 1, 2} in which no 0 is immediately followed by a 1 (no “01”). Find a recurrence for sn with initial conditions, and compute s5.

hard.answer: (a) aₙ = 2·3ⁿ + (−2)ⁿ (b) sₙ = 3sₙ₋₁ − sₙ₋₂, s₀ = 1, s₁ = 3; s₅ = 144

solution.title: Method
items: Characteristic equation: r² − r − 6 = 0, (r − 3)(r + 2) = 0, roots 3 and −2.
General solution: a<sub>n</sub> = α·3<sup>n</sup> + β·(−2)<sup>n</sup>.
a<sub>0</sub>: α + β = 3. a<sub>1</sub>: 3α − 2β = 4. Adding 2×(first): 5α = 10, α = 2, β = 1.
an = 2·3n + (−2)n. Check a2: recurrence 4 + 18 = 22; formula 18 + 4 = 22. ✓

solution.text: (b) Split valid strings of length n ≥ 2 by their last character.

solution.title: Method
items: Ends in 0 or 2: any valid string of length n − 1, then that character (appending 0 or 2 can’t create “01”): 2s<sub>n−1</sub>.

Ends in 1: a valid string of length n − 1 that does not end in 0, then 1. Valid strings of length n − 1 ending in 0 are just valid strings of length n − 2 followed by 0: there are sn−2 of them. So this case gives sn−1 − sn−2.
Total: sn = 3sn−1 − sn−2 for n ≥ 2, with s0 = 1 (empty string), s1 = 3.
Check s<sub>2</sub> = 9 − 1 = 8: all 9 strings except 01. ✓

solution.text: (Fun: these are every other Fibonacci number.)
Solving a linear homogeneous recurrence with distinct roots, and building a recurrence by conditioning on the last character.

In (b), claiming the strings ending in 1 number 2s<sub>n−2</sub> or s<sub>n−1</sub>. Always test the recurrence on a case you can count by hand (s<sub>2</sub> = 8). If you start from s<sub>1</sub>, s<sub>2</sub> instead of s<sub>0</sub>, that’s fine too.

keyFacts: Degree-k recurrence needs k initial conditions; check a closed form by plugging in
Model by splitting on the last (or first) step into disjoint cases
aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + ⋯ + cₖaₙ₋ₖ → characteristic equation rᵏ − c₁rᵏ⁻¹ − ⋯ − cₖ = 0
Root r of multiplicity m contributes (α₀ + α₁n + ⋯ + αₘ₋₁nᵐ⁻¹)rⁿ
Nonhomogeneous: aₙ = particular + homogeneous; apply initial conditions last
F(n) = p(n)sⁿ: try nᵐ·q(n)sⁿ, m = multiplicity of s as a root (resonance)
Hanoi Hₙ = 2ⁿ − 1; no-00 bit strings and 2 × n domino tilings are Fibonacci

parsons.title: Characteristic roots give solutions
parsons.goal: If r₁, r₂ are roots of r² − c₁r − c₂ = 0, then aₙ = α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ satisfies aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ for any constants α₁, α₂.
lines: Let r be a root of r² − c₁r − c₂ = 0, so r² = c₁r + c₂.
Multiply both sides by rⁿ⁻²: rⁿ = c₁rⁿ⁻¹ + c₂rⁿ⁻², so aₙ = rⁿ is a solution; in particular r₁ⁿ and r₂ⁿ are solutions.
For aₙ = α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ, regroup: c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ = α₁(c₁r₁ⁿ⁻¹ + c₂r₁ⁿ⁻²) + α₂(c₁r₂ⁿ⁻¹ + c₂r₂ⁿ⁻²).
Each bracket equals rᵢⁿ by the previous step applied to r = rᵢ.
So c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ = α₁r₁ⁿ + α₂r₂ⁿ = aₙ for every n ≥ 2. ∎
distractors: Let r be a root of r² + c₁r + c₂ = 0, so r² = −c₁r − c₂.
Multiply both sides by rⁿ: rⁿ⁺² = c₁rⁿ⁻¹ + c₂rⁿ⁻².
The combination is a solution only when α₁ = α₂ = 1.

parsons.title: Why a double root needs n·r₀ⁿ
parsons.goal: If r₀ is a double root of r² − c₁r − c₂ = 0, then aₙ = n·r₀ⁿ satisfies aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂.
lines: A double root means r² − c₁r − c₂ = (r − r₀)², so c₁ = 2r₀ and c₂ = −r₀².
Substitute aₙ = n·r₀ⁿ into the right side: c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ = 2r₀·(n − 1)r₀ⁿ⁻¹ − r₀²·(n − 2)r₀ⁿ⁻².
Collect the powers of r₀: this equals 2(n − 1)r₀ⁿ − (n − 2)r₀ⁿ.
So c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂ = n·r₀ⁿ = aₙ, and n·r₀ⁿ is a second, independent solution besides r₀ⁿ. ∎
distractors: A double root means c₁ = r₀² and c₂ = 2r₀.
Collect the powers of r₀: this equals 2(n − 1)r₀ⁿ − (n − 2)r₀ⁿ⁻¹.

parsons.title: Setting up a recurrence: no two consecutive 0s
parsons.goal: Let aₙ be the number of bit strings of length n with no two consecutive 0s. Show aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 3, with a₁ = 2, a₂ = 3.
lines: Take a valid string of length n ≥ 3 and split into cases by its last bit.
If it ends in 1, the first n − 1 bits can be any valid string of length n − 1: aₙ₋₁ strings.
If it ends in 0, the bit before it must be 1 (else 00 appears), and the first n − 2 bits can be any valid string: aₙ₋₂ strings.
The two cases are disjoint and cover every valid string, so by the sum rule aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂.
Initial conditions by listing: a₁ = 2 (0, 1) and a₂ = 3 (01, 10, 11). ∎
distractors: If it ends in 0, the first n − 1 bits can be any valid string: aₙ₋₁ strings.
The cases overlap in strings ending in 10, so aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ − aₙ₋₃.
Initial conditions by listing: a₁ = 2 and a₂ = 4.
